articles.body: NEW DELHI: Actor and BJP MP Kangana Ranaut has weighed in on the online controversy surrounding Kriti Sanonâs latest Raksha Bandhan advertisement, questioning the actorâs choice of outfit and asking why someone would tie a rakhi while dressed in a bikini-style ensemble.Kritiâs jewellery advertisement, released ahead of Raksha Bandhan, features her in an Indo-Western outfit comprising a bralette-inspired blouse, cape and draped skirt.The look has drawn criticism online, with some users arguing that it was out of place in an advertisement centred on the traditional festival celebrating the bond between siblings.Joining the debate, Kangana shared a note on her Instagram Story on Monday evening, questioning the styling choices in the advertisement.âIt's a wonderful time to be a woman. Our closets are full of variety of clothes, today's woman is a global woman. From cocktail dresses to lehenga cholis, jeans to saris, bikinis to salwar kameez, from all the options that are available to us today why would you tie your brother a rakhi in your bikini/undergarments? Where are all your styling options? Ha ha the advert looks intentionally creepy!â she wrote.The advertisement had already sparked a debate on social media, with several users criticising Kritiâs outfit and other elements of the campaign.One user on X questioned the absence of traditional elements associated with Raksha Bandhan, writing, âWhere is Puja Ki thali? Why are you wearing bra in front of your brother? Is this a Raksha Bandhan? Where is Tilak?âAnother criticised the outfit, writing, "Who dresses like this on rakhi ?"Kriti has not issued any statement on the criticism or Kanganaâs remarks so far.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Tech Town project equips Barnsley jobseekers with AI skills
articles.summary: New courses in Barnsley will offer training as well as paid work placements.
articles.body:
Barnsley residents will be offered support in using artificial intelligence (AI) to train for future careers under two new government schemes.

AI Career Launchpad will offer flexible training and paid work placements with employers, while Getting Job Ready with AI will support jobseekers, the Cabinet Office said.

The training comes six months after Barnsley was dubbed the UK's first "Tech Town", with firms including Microsoft, Cisco and Adobe pledging to support local people seeking "jobs of the future".

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: "AI is going to transform the world of work and our job is to make sure working people benefit from that change."

He added: "That starts with helping people understand how AI can be useful day-to-day - whether that means finding a job, learning new skills or building a career in a growing industry.

"Barnsley is showing what this can look like in practice.

"As our first Tech Town, it is helping us find ways that can create opportunities for local people and support communities across the country."

The AI Career Launchpad, a partnership with Barnsley College worth more than £400,000, will offer residents of all ages a faster, more flexible route into AI jobs.

Learners will get six months of training linked to a Level 4 apprenticeship, plus paid placements to gain experience while they learn.

Barnsley College Principal and CEO David Akeroyd said the scheme opened up careers that had, until now, been "concentrated elsewhere in the country".

Local businesses that sign up will benefit by getting early access to people training in AI, with government-funded placements helping them bring fresh skills into their teams.

Once the programme has been completed, its curriculum will then be freely available for other colleges and training providers elsewhere to use across the country.

From September, jobseekers in Barnsley will also get hands-on support through the Getting Job Ready with AI pilot.

Support would include using AI to search for suitable roles, tailor CVs and cover letters, prepare for interviews and understand how employers are already using digital tools in day-to-day jobs.

People will be referred onto the course through Jobcentre Plus.

The pilot forms part of a wider drive by the Department for Work and Pensions to get more people into work and help them progress once there, including reforming jobcentres into a universal careers service.

Matt O'Neill, Barnsley Council's Executive Director for Place, said the authority hoped the schemes would "make a real difference" to residents' lives.

"Tech Town is about using technology in ways that are inclusive, trusted and rooted in everyday life," he said.

"We want to make sure residents, employers and communities across the borough are ready for the jobs and services of the future."

Alongside the two new schemes, an assessment launching in autumn will look at how local charities, community groups and social enterprises are already using AI, and where further support could make the biggest difference.

Lessons from Barnsley will inform how similar approaches could be used elsewhere as the government works to equip 10 million UK workers with AI skills by 2030.

articles.title: In 2017, Florida scientists tested mosquitoes around Burmese pythons; three mosquito species contained python DNA in their blood meals, suggesting insects could help locate hidden giant snakes
articles.summary: US News: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the .
articles.body: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the most concerning invasive species in South Florida, as they can hide in dense vegetation, wetlands, and remote areas, making them notoriously difficult to find. Now, researchers have examined a strange strategy: allowing mosquitoes to discover where the giant snakes may be lurking. In the journal PLOS ONE, a study by Lawrence E. Reeves called "Interactions between the invasive Burmese python, Python bivittatus Kuhl, and the local mosquito community in Florida, USA," appears to suggest something beyond imagination, where it is thought that mosquitoes might become python detectives. The idea was based on doctoral research by Lawrence Reeves, a post-doctoral researcher at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Florida Medical Entomology Lab in Vero Beach. Reeves and his research team examined the interactions between Burmese pythons and mosquitoes, an ecological relationship that had been largely ignored. While the effects of pythons on the animals they eat are fairly obvious, we know much less about their interactions with animals that eat them or otherwise interact with them. The researchers collected mosquitoes from a Burmese python facility in Florida, where the snakes were housed in outdoor cages. And when they examined the blood within the mosquitoes, they found Burmese python DNA in the blood meals of three different species of mosquito. The discovery also opened up the unlikely possibility that mosquitoes could one day serve as biological trackers of hidden pythons. Scroll down for the details.How the technique would work"While a mosquito is feeding, it ingests blood from its host," the research paper reads. And if you can get the DNA from that blood meal, you might be able to tell what animal the insect was feeding on most recently. This means that mosquitoes caught in the wild could provide clues to the presence of Burmese pythons in an area. Rather than searching every marsh or clump of vegetation for a well-camouflaged snake, researchers could simply gather mosquitoes and test their blood meals for python DNA. This technique could be used to produce tiny biological surveillance devices from common insects.Why Burmese pythons are so hard to findBurmese pythons are a major detection challenge because they are extremely adept at avoiding humans, the study shows. Their coloration and semi-aquatic lifestyle provides them with camouflage and the ability to inhabit hard-to-reach wetlands and more remote habitats. They are large, and thus may seem easy to spot, but often the opposite is true. A python can hide itself in the vegetation or in places that are hard for people to reach.Researchers have tried various methods to locate the invasive snakes, including volunteers searching for pythons, specially trained detection dogs, and experienced snake hunters from Indiaâs Irula community. All methods have their limitations; manual searches can be time-consuming, and remote terrain makes access difficult. Mosquito-based detection could be another possible tool for identifying areas with pythons.From snake tracking to ecosystem surveysThe team believes the method can be used for more than just locating individual pythons. Testing mosquitoes for python DNA could help scientists track the invasive snakes and conduct biodiversity surveys. Mosquitoes can travel through areas that are hard for researchers to access directly, and they can potentially provide biological clues from places not easily reached by humans. The technique would not necessarily replace current methods of catching or removing pythons. Instead, it can help researchers narrow their search and identify places worth a closer look.Could mosquitoes spread diseases from pythons?This finding raises another important scientific question. Would mosquitoes that feed on Burmese pythons be able to pick up pathogens from the snakes and transmit them to other animals? Scientists have previously studied connections between mosquitoes, snakes and diseases. Other snakes are believed to be involved in transmission of viruses such as West Nile virus and Eastern equine encephalitis virus. Burmese pythons are also vulnerable to infection with some pathogens. Studies have found that snakes can become infected with the chikungunya virus and then infect mosquitoes, but the wider significance of this route is unknown. Thatâs why scientists want to know if mosquitoes feeding on Burmese pythons could help spread disease in the ecosystem of the Everglades.A little bug with a major potential roleThe finding illustrates how research on invasive species can go off in unexpected directions. A mosquito may be a tiny irritant compared to a giant python, but the blood it drinks can contain valuable genetic information about the animals itâs encountered. If researchers can make this approach work in the wild, mosquito surveillance could be another weapon in the fight to track Burmese pythons across South Florida. Right now the research is an interesting possibility: Instead of asking humans, dogs, or trained snake hunters to find the hidden pythons, scientists may be able to ask the mosquitoes where they have been.Images Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Pizza Hut and Josh Allen promise free pizza for life — but the fine print caps it at $10,800
articles.summary: The chain is going all-in on football season, also renaming itself simply "Hut."
articles.body:
Die-hard NFL fans might flock to Buffalo wings when they watch a game, but pizza is a close second. And Pizza Hut is looking to hook the faithful with a slew of football-themed promotions, including one that will award free pizza for life to three lucky fans.

The chain is teaming with Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen as a spokesperson this season — and to underscore its commitment to the game, Pizza Hut dropped the "Pizza" from its name on social media and some restaurant exteriors, temporarily calling itself "Hut."

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 moves to make before the window closes

(Don't get too comfortable with that name change. The company has already re-added "Pizza" on social media, though some restaurant locations may leave it blocked out for the entirety of the NFL season .)

As for the lifetime of pizza, "lifetime" might be doing a bit of heavy lifting in that phrase. The winners of the contest will receive 1 million Hut Rewards Points , which the company says has a cash value of $10,800. Pizza prices vary from city to city at the chain, but a large Meat Lover's or Supreme Pizza tends to come in at around $22. So, using that as a baseline, the points would pay for less than 500 pizzas. That's less than 10 years' worth if you get a pizza a week (and considerably shorter if you have college-aged kids).

Still, free food is free food. If you're interested in trying to win one of the three prizes, head to pizzahut.com/gamedaystartswithhut and upload a video of yourself saying "HUT" in your best QB voice, showing some sort of action (i.e. snapping the ball, having a watch party, calling the snap count). You'll also have to explain in a few words why gameday starts with a HUT for you.

Pizza Hut doesn't specifically say you can't use AI in creating the video, but it made it pretty clear that's a no-no in the fine print.

"Entry Videos must: (a) be the original work product of Participant; (b) be solely owned by Participant and with no other person or entity having any right or interest in it; and (c) not violate any third-party rights including but not limited to copyright, trademark, patent, contract, and/or publicity or privacy rights, of any other person or entity," the rules read.

articles.title: A Kansas cowboy put 50 wind turbines on his 7,000-acre ranch and turned the wind into his most reliable cash crop, selling electricity to thousands of homes
articles.summary: US News: A 7,000-acre cattle ranch in Kansas has found an unusual way to generate a steady income alongside traditional ranching. Pete Ferrell, a fourth-genera.
articles.body: A 7,000-acre cattle ranch in Kansas has found an unusual way to generate a steady income alongside traditional ranching. Pete Ferrell, a fourth-generation rancher, hosts 50 industrial wind turbines on his property as part of the 100-turbine Elk River Wind Project, a 150-megawatt facility that began operating in 2005. The turbines do not replace the cattle or transform the entire ranch into an energy facility. Instead, cattle continue to graze across much of the tallgrass prairie while the wind project provides Ferrell with lease income. The facility also generates enough electricity to serve tens of thousands of homes based on its original production estimates. What began as a source of concern for Ferrell eventually became an important financial cushion, particularly during droughts when traditional ranching income can become unpredictable.A Kansas cowboy turns 50 wind turbines into a new cash cropThe Ferrell family's connection to wind power began long before today's giant turbines appeared across Kansas. In 1923, Ferrell's great-grandfather installed a Jacobs Windjammer wind turbine paired with a Delco glass battery at the ranch, providing electricity before the electrical grid reached the property. Nearly a century later, Pete Ferrell faced a very different proposal when developers approached him about installing commercial wind turbines. He initially rejected the idea because he feared the machines would damage the prairie and interfere with the ranching operation. A visit to California's Altamont Pass changed his perspective after he saw ranchers continuing to care for their land while turbines operated around them. The experience helped convince Ferrell that wind energy could coexist with cattle ranching, eventually leading him to lease part of his property for the Elk River Wind Project.Fifty turbines are part of a 100-turbine wind farmThe 50 turbines on Ferrell's property represent only half of the Elk River Wind Project. Kansas state records describe the facility as a 150-megawatt wind farm containing 100 GE 1.5-megawatt turbines in Butler County near Beaumont. The remaining turbines are located on neighbouring properties. The project began commercial operation in December 2005 and was originally expected to generate about 550,000 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. At the time, developers estimated that output would be equivalent to the electricity consumption of roughly 42,000 homes annually. The actual amount of electricity produced varies depending on wind conditions, so the figure should be understood as an annual estimate rather than a fixed number of homes receiving power directly from Ferrell's turbines. The electricity enters the regional power system, while Ferrell receives income from leasing his land to the project.Wind became a reliable source of ranch incomeThe biggest attraction for Ferrell was not simply the electricity produced by the turbines but the additional income generated by leasing his land. Wind royalties have become an important part of the ranch's finances, providing a source of revenue that does not depend directly on cattle prices, grass production or rainfall. Ferrell has described wind as his "best insurance policy" because the payments continue even during difficult agricultural years. Drought can reduce forage across the Flint Hills and force ranchers to reduce livestock numbers or spend more money on feed, while the turbines can continue producing electricity as long as suitable winds are available. The arrangement effectively allows the same land to generate two forms of economic value. Cattle continue to provide the traditional agricultural income, while the wind project provides lease payments. The Environmental Defense Fund has highlighted Ferrell's experience as an example of how renewable-energy development can provide financial stability for rural landowners.Cattle still graze around the turbinesThe presence of 50 industrial turbines has not ended the ranch's traditional agricultural operation. Cattle continue to graze across much of the property, including areas surrounding the turbine infrastructure. Ferrell has said that roughly 50 acres of the ranch became unavailable for grazing because of turbine foundations, roads and related infrastructure. That represents only a small portion of a property covering about 7,000 acres. The arrangement allows Ferrell to maintain cattle production while earning additional revenue from the wind project. This is particularly significant in the Flint Hills, where ranching depends heavily on the health of native tallgrass prairie and seasonal weather conditions. Wind development therefore became an additional layer of income rather than a replacement for agriculture. Ferrell's experience shows why some rural landowners view turbines differently from people who see them only as large industrial structures. On a working ranch, the infrastructure can occupy a relatively small part of the property while providing payments over many years.The project brought wider economic benefits to the regionElk River is part of Kansas's much larger wind-energy industry, which has brought significant investment and lease payments to rural communities. Wind projects can generate revenue for landowners while also contributing to local tax bases, construction activity and employment. Kansas has become one of the leading wind-energy states in the US because of its strong wind resources and large areas of relatively open land. The economic benefits, however, come alongside genuine debates about where turbines should be built. Residents and landowners can raise concerns about views, wildlife, noise, roads, transmission infrastructure and changes to rural landscapes. Those issues are particularly important in the Flint Hills because the region contains some of the largest remaining areas of tallgrass prairie in North America. Ferrell's experience should therefore not be treated as evidence that every ranch is suitable for wind development. Instead, it shows how carefully planned projects can coexist with agricultural operations and give landowners another source of income.The wind became another cash crop without replacing the cattleNearly two decades after the Elk River Wind Project began operating, Ferrell's ranch remains a working cattle operation with 50 turbines standing across its prairie. The electricity generated by those turbines is sold into the regional power system, rather than directly by Ferrell to individual households, while his income comes from leasing his land to the wind project. That distinction does not make the financial transformation any less remarkable. The ranch has effectively found a way to make the same landscape produce two different sources of economic value. Cattle still depend on grass, rainfall and market conditions, while the wind turbines provide a separate stream of lease revenue. The arrangement also reflects a much longer family relationship with wind power that began with a small turbine and battery in 1923. Almost a century later, the Ferrell family is still drawing value from the Kansas wind, only now on a vastly larger scale.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

A visit to California's Altamont Pass changed his perspective after he saw ranchers continuing to care for their land while turbines operated around them. The experience helped convince Ferrell that wind energy could coexist with cattle ranching, eventually leading him to lease part of his property for the Elk River Wind Project.Fifty turbines are part of a 100-turbine wind farmThe 50 turbines on Ferrell's property represent only half of the Elk River Wind Project. Kansas state records describe the facility as a 150-megawatt wind farm containing 100 GE 1.5-megawatt turbines in Butler County near Beaumont. The remaining turbines are located on neighbouring properties. The project began commercial operation in December 2005 and was originally expected to generate about 550,000 megawatt-hours of electricity each year. At the time, developers estimated that output would be equivalent to the electricity consumption of roughly 42,000 homes annually. The actual amount of electricity produced varies depending on wind conditions, so the figure should be understood as an annual estimate rather than a fixed number of homes receiving power directly from Ferrell's turbines. The electricity enters the regional power system, while Ferrell receives income from leasing his land to the project.Wind became a reliable source of ranch incomeThe biggest attraction for Ferrell was not simply the electricity produced by the turbines but the additional income generated by leasing his land. Wind royalties have become an important part of the ranch's finances, providing a source of revenue that does not depend directly on cattle prices, grass production or rainfall. Ferrell has described wind as his "best insurance policy" because the payments continue even during difficult agricultural years. Drought can reduce forage across the Flint Hills and force ranchers to reduce livestock numbers or spend more money on feed, while the turbines can continue producing electricity as long as suitable winds are available. The arrangement effectively allows the same land to generate two forms of economic value. Cattle continue to provide the traditional agricultural income, while the wind project provides lease payments. The Environmental Defense Fund has highlighted Ferrell's experience as an example of how renewable-energy development can provide financial stability for rural landowners.Cattle still graze around the turbinesThe presence of 50 industrial turbines has not ended the ranch's traditional agricultural operation. Cattle continue to graze across much of the property, including areas surrounding the turbine infrastructure. Ferrell has said that roughly 50 acres of the ranch became unavailable for grazing because of turbine foundations, roads and related infrastructure. That represents only a small portion of a property covering about 7,000 acres. The arrangement allows Ferrell to maintain cattle production while earning additional revenue from the wind project. This is particularly significant in the Flint Hills, where ranching depends heavily on the health of native tallgrass prairie and seasonal weather conditions. Wind development therefore became an additional layer of income rather than a replacement for agriculture. Ferrell's experience shows why some rural landowners view turbines differently from people who see them only as large industrial structures. On a working ranch, the infrastructure can occupy a relatively small part of the property while providing payments over many years.The project brought wider economic benefits to the regionElk River is part of Kansas's much larger wind-energy industry, which has brought significant investment and lease payments to rural communities. Wind projects can generate revenue for landowners while also contributing to local tax bases, construction activity and employment. Kansas has become one of the leading wind-energy states in the US because of its strong wind resources and large areas of relatively open land. The economic benefits, however, come alongside genuine debates about where turbines should be built. Residents and landowners can raise concerns about views, wildlife, noise, roads, transmission infrastructure and changes to rural landscapes. Those issues are particularly important in the Flint Hills because the region contains some of the largest remaining areas of tallgrass prairie in North America. Ferrell's experience should therefore not be treated as evidence that every ranch is suitable for wind development. Instead, it shows how carefully planned projects can coexist with agricultural operations and give landowners another source of income.The wind became another cash crop without replacing the cattleNearly two decades after the Elk River Wind Project began operating, Ferrell's ranch remains a working cattle operation with 50 turbines standing across its prairie. The electricity generated by those turbines is sold into the regional power system, rather than directly by Ferrell to individual households, while his income comes from leasing his land to the wind project. That distinction does not make the financial transformation any less remarkable. The ranch has effectively found a way to make the same landscape produce two different sources of economic value. Cattle still depend on grass, rainfall and market conditions, while the wind turbines provide a separate stream of lease revenue. The arrangement also reflects a much longer family relationship with wind power that began with a small turbine and battery in 1923. Almost a century later, the Ferrell family is still drawing value from the Kansas wind, only now on a vastly larger scale.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran has closed the vital waterway since the beginning of the conflict causing wild fluctuations in oil prices worldwide.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

Iran, for its part, has indicated that it wants to establish full control of the Strait of Hormuz - a view that is opposed by the US and most other countries which believe that the passage constitutes international waters and transit should remain unimpeded as it was before the war.

Until recently - and on the basis of the MoU - Iran had been involved in negotiations with Oman, a US ally, to agree a mechanism for administering the strait. However, those talks have so far not produced an agreement and, last week, Trump even threatened to bomb its ally "if it gets in the way" of his administration's own talks with Iran over the issue.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the strait after meeting his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.

He said in a statement he also hoped for "practical arrangements" to restore safe navigation, adding: "Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course."

Araghchi confirmed the meeting in a statement, saying "regional solutions" were discussed in talks with representatives from Pakistan and Oman.

He added that discussions covered the future management of the strait, as well as the framework for a new corridor and a joint mine-clearing operation.

Speaking to state television news after the meeting Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabad said the entry route to the Gulf would be "through Iranian waters and the exit route through Omani territorial waters, and ships will pass through Iranian waters on both routes".

The minister added that the south corridor of the waterway, which has been recommended to shipping firms by the US and is situated close to the coast of Oman , would be "closed" under the framework, and the meeting "does not mean that the Strait will be opened from tomorrow".

He said "no military vessels will be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and only commercial vessels will be allowed to pass through it".

Gharibabad called the route "temporary", adding Iran and Oman will negotiate a new permanent route within a timeframe of 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic plan.

"If Iran's requests are not granted, the Strait will be closed," he said.

Why the Strait of Hormuz matters so much in the Iran war

Trump hopes sanctions will topple Iran's regime - its leaders are betting otherwise

China hits out at 'illegal' new US sanctions on Iran and trading partners

articles.title: 'Zero self-awareness': Indian-origin professor slams viral video of woman welcoming parents at US airport triggering wheelchair row
articles.summary: US News: Videos of Indians using wheelchairs at international airports surface on social media from time to time. This time, a video of an Indian woman apparen.
articles.body: Videos of Indians using wheelchairs at international airports surface on social media from time to time. This time, a video of an Indian woman apparently welcoming her parents at Dallas-Fort Worth Airport in Texas went viral as the mother was seen emerging from the airport in a wheelchair. But later she was walking."Dallas Fort Worth airport needs to publish its recovery statistics. Arrives needing a wheelchair and two airport employees. Leaves walking after all five suitcases have been handled. Remarkable medicine," an X post sharing the video commented sarcastically. It also mentioned that the video was on a public platform.The video went viral amid massive backlash targeted at Indians and Indian parents, while many explained why the wheelchairs are not only meant for disability but also for travel anxiety, long waiting, changes in schedules etc.Indian-origin professor Gaurav Sabnis slammed the 'scammy mindset' and observed that the woman didn't even think twice before posting the video. "Shows how normalized the scammy mindset has become in our culture in recent years. This woman didn't even have a thought before posting it that she was giving evidence of her parents using wheelchairs as a "jugaad". That this could go viral for that fact. Zero self-awareness," Prof Sabnis noted.Sabnis also countered factors like 'travel anxiety' and said that people from other countries too face anxiety, but wheelchairs are mostly abused by Indians. "Flaunting it on social media shows the extent of the moral rot in today's Indian elite," he commented. "Aren't there older adults from other countries flying places?" he asked."I've been traveling multiple times a year for many years and this wasn't common in 2012 for example where you still had a lot of senior citizens landing at Newark for their kids. This is a jugaad actively spread using Whatsapp and social media," he later explained.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: H-1B contracting firms under stricter scrutiny in new regulation: 'Why no new regulation for H-2B who work at Mar-a-Lago'
articles.summary: US News: Among a bunch of new changes that the Donald Trump administration is bringing to the H-1B visa program, the Department of Homeland Security also wants.
articles.body: Among a bunch of new changes that the Donald Trump administration is bringing to the H-1B visa program, the Department of Homeland Security also wants to provide greater scrutiny of third-party placements. It is a common practice in the H-1B visa program that a company hires a foreign worker on this visa program to perform jobs for another company. Such companies are also called IT bodyshops. These companies manage the payroll of the H-1B visa holders, and they handle the immigration filings of these visa holders while these visa holders work for another company. The end client, the company for which the H-1B visa holders work, basically outsources all the foreign hiring-related work to these third-party companies.This system breeds a lot of malpractice, as sometimes these staffing companies stop salaries and threaten the visa holders.The DHS said it would revise the eligibility for cap exemptions.Once the proposal is published in the Federal Register, DHS will accept public comments for 30 or 60 days.Why so much attention on H-1B and no attention to H2BThe H-1B visa program has dominated headlines in the second Trump administration so far. While Donald Trump promised before the election that he would staple Green Card to the degrees of foreign students, the administration took one step after another to make it difficult for foreign students to come to the US to study, and then start working and eventually to join the US workforce. The administration brought new rules at every step, leading to questions as to why the administration is only concentrating on H-1B and not H-2B.H-2B is a work visa that allows employers to temporarily hire nonimmigrants to perform non-agricultural labor or services in the US. These visa workers can be employed for housekeeping, janitors, concierges, tree trimmers, irrigation labor, construction workers, etc. No degree is required."Why is the Trump administration actually increasing the number of H-2B visas? No fees, no controversy? These are for lower skilled workers who do take jobs away and do nothing for competitiveness... only cheap labor," Indian-American investor Vivek Wadhwa asked.Immigration commentator James Blunt said the administration is making it easier to import temporary labor but not high-skilled people who would innovate, build companies, and pay taxes. "Weâre making it easier to import temporary labor while making it brutally expensive to retain highly skilled people who could spend decades working, paying taxes, innovating and building companies in America. Thatâs the economic stupidity Iâm pointing out," Blunt said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Iran and Oman negotiate joint Strait of Hormuz shipping corridor
articles.summary: The two countries are also discussing a joint mine-clearing mission, even as President Trump said the U.S. Navy had already removed all mines from the waterw...
articles.body:
Iran and Oman met on Tuesday to negotiate a temporary joint shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, along with a mission to clear mines from the critical oil export route.

Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi called his meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi in Tehran productive, expressing optimism that a temporary corridor and "practical arrangements to restore safe navigation" would be unveiled in short order. Oman's Foreign Ministry posted on social media that the framework under discussion envisions a joint mine-clearing effort, with both nations committed to further talks aimed at establishing a lasting corridor and governance structure for the strait.

The diplomats did not reach a deal, according to Axios . In a joint statement, Iran and Oman said they are also discussing a mechanism for information exchange, traffic management, and maritime and security services.

The talks came on the same day President Donald Trump announced that the U.S. Navy had completed its own mine-removal operation. "I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz," Trump wrote on Truth Social. He warned that Iran has been put on notice that any vessel caught laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed," and he noted that the U.S. Space Force has the waterway under surveillance.

Oman's reference to a mine-clearing mission appeared to contradict Trump's statement, according to CNBC . Axios reported that two U.S. officials with direct knowledge of the operation corroborated Trump's claim, adding that the Navy spent several months deploying underwater drones to scan the Traffic Separation Scheme — the median lane of the strait — and identified more than 100 objects believed to be mines, which private contractors were then hired to remove or destroy.

The Iran-Oman discussions come against a backdrop of U.S. military escorts enabling tankers to move more than 660 million barrels of crude through the strait since early May , though throughput remains well below the roughly 20 million barrels per day the waterway handled before the conflict. Traffic has been routed through a southern lane hugging the Omani coastline, with U.S. officials telling Axios that the channel handled over 500 ship transits in the preceding month.

The Iran-Oman talks followed by one day Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's warning that the U.S. would impose sanctions on any nation conducting business with Iran, according to CNBC. Trump earlier this month threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way."

articles.title: Dolly Parton, singer-songwriter, 1946-2026
articles.summary: Dolly Parton was at once larger than life and down to earth. The Nashville star, who has died aged 80, was a vision of fabulous folksiness with...
articles.body:
Dolly Parton was at once larger than life and down to earth. The Nashville star, who has died aged 80, was a vision of fabulous folksiness with her blonde wigs, rhinestones and dazzling smile. She wrote songs in industrial quantities, about 3,000 in her estimation, but performed them with a very human wit and warmth. With more than 100mn record sales to her name and a renown stretching far beyond the boundaries of her genre, she ranks among the greatest artists in the history of country music.

She was born in rural Tennessee in 1946, at the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains. Her father was a sharecropper who later became a tobacco farmer. Her mother had 12 children, including Parton, by the age of 35. It was an impoverished upbringing. According to Parton, her penniless father paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. "I have often joked that I have been raking in the dough ever since," she wrote in her autobiography, Dolly: My Life and Other Unfinished Business .

There was neither self-pity nor selfishness in her passage from rags to riches. She sang about being mocked by schoolmates for wearing a coat made from scraps of fabric in "Coat of Many Colors". "I couldn't understand it, for I felt I was rich," Parton sang in the 1971 signature song. "And I told them of the love my momma sewed in every stitch." At this point in the song, a key change lifts us up too.

She could dole out schmaltz with the best of them, although she was a sophisticated singer and songwriter too. Drawn to music from a young age, she was brought up amid the music of church and family gatherings rather than records or radio. After graduating from high school, she left home for Nashville in 1964. Another autobiographical song, "The Letter", evokes the small-town girl's first weeks in Music City, singing on morning television shows and writing hits for other acts.

Her first country hit as a recording artist came in 1967 with the single "Dumb Blonde". "This dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool," she sang. It was penned by another Nashville songwriter, but the mix of self-mockery and defiance was typical of Parton . Country music's tradition of strong womanhood allowed a certain degree of challenge to its even more powerful culture of sexism. Parton was audacious yet also astute in testing the limits that she faced.

Initially, her extravagantly quivering voice was divisive. "I just don't think the girl can sing," a record executive told Nashville veteran Porter Wagoner when he proposed teaming with Parton as a duo in 1967. Wagoner insisted, and the partnership was a success. It provided the platform for her solo career to blossom in the early 1970s with hits such as "Coat of Many Colors".

Drawn to music from a young age, she was brought up amid the music of church and family gatherings rather than records or radio. After graduating from high school, she left home for Nashville in 1964. Another autobiographical song, "The Letter", evokes the small-town girl's first weeks in Music City, singing on morning television shows and writing hits for other acts.

Her first country hit as a recording artist came in 1967 with the single "Dumb Blonde". "This dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool," she sang. It was penned by another Nashville songwriter, but the mix of self-mockery and defiance was typical of Parton . Country music's tradition of strong womanhood allowed a certain degree of challenge to its even more powerful culture of sexism. Parton was audacious yet also astute in testing the limits that she faced.

Initially, her extravagantly quivering voice was divisive. "I just don't think the girl can sing," a record executive told Nashville veteran Porter Wagoner when he proposed teaming with Parton as a duo in 1967. Wagoner insisted, and the partnership was a success. It provided the platform for her solo career to blossom in the early 1970s with hits such as "Coat of Many Colors".

articles.title: 2026 Little League World Series: Scores, schedule, results, bracket as tournament continues in Williamsport
articles.summary: The Little League World Series is back.
articles.body:
The Little League World Series officially kicked off Wednesday, with the 20-team field finalized, featuring 10 U.S. teams and 10 international teams seeking a championship.

The tournament is back in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, once again this year, where all games will be held at Howard J. Lamade or Volunteer Stadium. Both the United States and International sides will play out double-elimination brackets until two teams from each bracket are left standing.

The remaining four teams will play in international and U.S. championship games on Aug. 29. The winner of those two games will advance to play in the championship game on Aug. 30. The losers of the semifinals will play in the third-place game.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest from the LLWS, including each day's schedule and results.

articles.title: San Antonio Spurs Have Bright Future Directly in Sight
articles.summary: The 2026-27 San Antonio Spurs season is one that is facing sky-high expectations.The Spurs are coming off of a defeat in the 2026 NBA Finals. The sobering lo...
articles.body:
The 2026-27 San Antonio Spurs season is one that is facing sky-high expectations.

The Spurs are coming off of a defeat in the 2026 NBA Finals. The sobering loss isn't lessening hopes of bringing the first title to San Antonio since 2014, however.

The championship aspirations are extending beyond this season as well. The blend of present expectations and future anticipation should undeniably excite Spurs fans.

Getty Dylan Harper is posturing to have a year two breakout.

The Spurs' future is extremely bright according to the consensus. Stephen Noh of Sporting News is further asserting this sentiment, as he projects the Spurs as the number one team in the NBA three years down the line.

San Antonio ranks directly ahead of Western Conference rivals in the Oklahoma City Thunder and Los Angeles Lakers here. This is an incredible vote of confidence in a franchise that still faces challenges despite being lush with assets.

Victor Wembanyama taking a discount in his rookie-scale contract makes it much more simple to build a sufficient roster around him. Dylan Harper is already establishing himself as one of the brightest two-way stars at the guard position in the league ( Crafted NBA ). Breakout star Stephon Castle is ready to take another step in year three in his own right.

This isn't even including the likes of Devin Vassell , Keldon Johnson , and the war chest of draft picks that should be in tow.

One potential downside for the Spurs is likely needing to part ways with draft assets to trade De'Aaron Fox away. While the trade for Fox made since at the time, Harper's emergence opens the door to fully commit to him long-term. The contract Fox is in control of will be difficult to move without attaching draft capital in all likelihood.

Center Luke Kornet is a win-now mode, as well as forwards Harrison Barnes and Tobias Harris . These players give San Antonio value in the moment without sacrificing future flexibility.

GettyStephon Castle is the perfect third star for San Antonio.

Oklahoma City is nearly as flush with controllable assets as San Antonio is, which sets the stage for a heavyweight battle for years to come.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is entering the season as the consensus top player in the league. Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren are both high-level stars and potential trade chips. Oklahoma City's trade asset chest is on-par with the Spurs' as well. San Antonio head coach Mitch Johnson is one of the brightest rising minds in the NBA. Oklahoma City head coach Mark Daigneault is already a champion, while setting the stage for even more growth.

The two franchises – in many ways – mirror one another. While San Antonio is a safe bet to be the best team in the league in three years, Oklahoma City has just as strong of a case. This is especially driven by the Thunder's ability to draft, which is fueled by GM Sam Presti's astute nature.

The playoff series in May simply served as a prelude for what is to come.
